---
title: "The Minnesota prior"
subtitle: "Lecture 6"
---

## Overview

By the end of this lecture you can estimate a system with more coefficients than
the sample can support, and say exactly how much of the least-squares answer the
prior has kept.

::: {.callout-important}
## The result of this chapter

For a linear system $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim
\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2 I_n)$ and a Normal prior $\beta \sim \mathcal{N}(b_0, B_0)$,
the posterior mean is the least-squares estimate passed through a matrix,

$$
\mathbb{E}[\beta \mid y] = W\,\hat\beta_{\text{OLS}} + (I_k - W)\,b_0,
\qquad
W = \left(\frac{X^\top X}{\sigma^2} + B_0^{-1}\right)^{-1}\frac{X^\top X}{\sigma^2},
$$

so each coefficient is a compromise between data and prior whose weights are the
two precisions rather than a tuning choice. The difficulty is that $W$ is not a
scalar. It pulls hardest along the directions the design measures worst, and
choosing $B_0$ is what decides where those directions lie.
:::

After working through this chapter you can

1. diagnose why least squares fails when the number of coefficients approaches the
   number of observations, in terms of the eigenvalues of the design;
2. derive the Normal posterior mean as a matrix-weighted average of the prior mean
   and the least-squares estimate;
3. derive the Minnesota prior variance from statements about units, lag decay and
   where the sample is informative;
4. implement the Minnesota posterior mean for a vector autoregression in Python and
   compare it with least squares coefficient by coefficient;
5. compare shrunk and unrestricted forecasts out of sample against a random walk and
   a univariate benchmark;
6. interpret the overall tightness as the dial that trades bias against variance, and
   predict how its value should move as the sample grows.

Week 6 of 15, paired with the [Week 6 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/06-minnesota-priors.qmd). The chapter assumes the
Normal linear regression posterior of Lecture 2 and the matrix algebra of completing
a square; the samplers of Lectures 4 and 5 are not needed, because everything here is
available in closed form.

## Motivation: a hundred and eleven coefficients on a hundred and twenty months {#sec-motivation}

A central bank forecasts output, prices and its own policy rate together, because the
three move as a system: the rate responds to inflation, inflation responds to
activity, and activity responds to the rate. The standard vehicle is a vector
autoregression, in which each variable is regressed on twelve monthly lags of all
three. Twelve lags is not extravagance. Monthly macroeconomic data carry seasonal
structure and policy transmits over roughly a year, so a shorter lag length throws
away the mechanism the model exists to describe.

The arithmetic is the problem. With $m = 3$ variables and $p = 12$ lags each equation
has $1 + mp = 37$ coefficients and the system has $111$. A decade of monthly data,
the natural window when one wants a single monetary regime rather than an average of
several, supplies $120$ usable observations. That is $3.24$ observations per
coefficient, and the chunk below shows what least squares does with them. It fits the
decade from January 1990 to December 1999, taken from the monthly panel described in
@sec-data, and then applies that fixed fit one month ahead over the following decade.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

DATA = next(p for p in (Path("data"), Path("../data")) if p.exists())
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.figsize": (7, 4.2), "axes.grid": True,
                     "grid.alpha": 0.3, "font.size": 11})

fred = pd.read_parquet(DATA / "fred_macro_monthly.parquet")
mac = pd.DataFrame({
    "ip_growth": 100 * np.log(fred["industrial_prod"]).diff(),
    "inflation": 100 * np.log(fred["cpi"]).diff(),
    "fed_funds": fred["fed_funds"],
}).dropna()
var_names, m_var, p_var = list(mac.columns), 3, 12

def build_var_xy(data, p):                 # stacked regression form of a VAR(p)
    T, m = data.shape
    Y = data[p:]
    X = np.ones((T - p, 1 + m * p))
    for ell in range(1, p + 1):
        X[:, 1 + (ell - 1) * m: 1 + ell * m] = data[p - ell: T - ell]
    return X, Y

est_start, est_end = "1989-01", "1999-12"          # 12 lags plus 120 response months
win = mac.loc[est_start:est_end].to_numpy()
X_var, Y_var = build_var_xy(win, p_var)
k_var = X_var.shape[1]

B_ols_var = np.linalg.solve(X_var.T @ X_var, X_var.T @ Y_var)
resid_in = Y_var - X_var @ B_ols_var
sd_in = resid_in.std(axis=0)

X_out, Y_out = build_var_xy(mac.loc["1999-01":"2009-12"].to_numpy(), p_var)
sd_out = np.sqrt(((Y_out - X_out @ B_ols_var) ** 2).mean(axis=0))
nxt = mac.loc["2000-01":"2009-12"].to_numpy()
sd_rw = np.sqrt(((nxt[1:] - nxt[:-1]) ** 2).mean(axis=0))

XtX_inv = np.linalg.inv(X_var.T @ X_var)
sig2_in = resid_in.var(axis=0) * X_var.shape[0] / (X_var.shape[0] - k_var)
se_ols = np.sqrt(np.outer(np.diag(XtX_inv), sig2_in))
tstat = B_ols_var[1:] / se_ols[1:]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 4.0))
lag_index = np.repeat(np.arange(1, p_var + 1), m_var)
for eq in range(m_var):
    axes[0].errorbar(lag_index + 0.22 * (eq - 1), B_ols_var[1:, eq],
                     yerr=2 * se_ols[1:, eq], fmt="o", ms=3, lw=0.8,
                     alpha=0.7, color=f"C{eq}", label=var_names[eq])
axes[0].axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
axes[0].set_xlabel("lag"); axes[0].set_ylabel("least-squares coefficient")
axes[0].set_title("108 lag coefficients, two standard errors"); axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)

pos = np.arange(m_var)
axes[1].bar(pos - 0.26, sd_in, width=0.26, label="in sample, 1990s")
axes[1].bar(pos, sd_out, width=0.26, label="one step ahead, 2000s")
axes[1].bar(pos + 0.26, sd_rw, width=0.26, label="random walk, 2000s")
axes[1].set_xticks(pos); axes[1].set_xticklabels(var_names, fontsize=8)
axes[1].set_ylabel("root mean squared error")
axes[1].set_title("The fit does not travel"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"{X_var.shape[0]} observations, {k_var} coefficients per equation, "
      f"{k_var * m_var} in the system, {X_var.shape[0] / k_var:.2f} per coefficient")
print(f"in-sample residual sd:      {np.round(sd_in, 4)}")
print(f"one-step-ahead RMSE 2000s:  {np.round(sd_out, 4)}")
print(f"random walk RMSE 2000s:     {np.round(sd_rw, 4)}")
print(f"share of lag coefficients with |t| < 1: {np.mean(np.abs(tstat) < 1):.3f}")
print(f"largest |lag coefficient|: {np.abs(B_ols_var[1:]).max():.3f}")
```

The left panel is the fitted system. There are $108$ lag coefficients, the largest of
them $1.598$ in absolute value, and they show no tendency to shrink as the lag grows:
the coefficient on a variable eleven months ago is on average as large as the
coefficient on the same variable last month. Their error bars are enormous, and
$62.0$ percent of them have a $t$ statistic below one in absolute value, which is to say
the sample cannot tell most of them from zero. The largest of them, $-1.598$ on the
second lag of the funds rate in the output equation, asserts that a one point rise in
the policy rate two months ago cuts this month's industrial production growth by more
than one and a half percent, which no macroeconomist would defend.

The right panel is what that costs. In sample the model looks excellent: residual
standard deviations of $0.4066$, $0.1124$ and $0.1101$ against raw series standard
deviations of $0.5262$, $0.1683$ and $1.7753$ in the same window, so it explains more
than ninety-nine percent of the variance of the funds rate. Applied one step ahead over
the following decade the same coefficients give root mean squared errors of $1.1345$,
$0.4070$ and $0.2532$, between two and four times the in-sample figures, and worse on
every variable than a random walk that predicts no change at all, which manages
$0.9351$, $0.3876$ and $0.2261$.

The obvious response is to use a shorter lag length or fewer variables, and it is worth
saying why that is not the repair. Dropping to three lags would leave $10$ coefficients per
equation and a comfortable twelve observations each, but the model would then be unable to
represent the year-long transmission lag that is the whole reason a central bank builds it,
and the seasonal structure in monthly data would be pushed into the residuals. Dropping a
variable is worse, because the funds rate, output and prices are exactly the three things
the question is about. Every reduction that makes least squares behave also removes part of
the object being modelled, which is a poor trade when the alternative is to keep the model
and be more careful about what one is willing to believe about its coefficients.

That is the breakdown. A model that explains the past almost perfectly is beaten out of
sample by the rule that says nothing ever changes. Nothing is wrong with the
likelihood, and the next section shows that nothing is wrong with the estimator either,
in the sense that it is doing exactly what it was asked to do. What is wrong is the
asking.

## The problem: the design has directions the sample cannot see {#sec-problem}

### Result R-6.1: the variance of least squares, and why some shrinkage always helps

Let $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I_n)$ and
$X$ of full column rank $k$. Write $X^\top X = QDQ^\top$ with $Q$ orthogonal and
$D = \operatorname{diag}(d_1,\dots,d_k)$, and let $\gamma = Q^\top\beta$ be the
coefficients in the eigenbasis. Then the least-squares estimator has

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\|\hat\beta_{\text{OLS}} - \beta\|^2\right]
= \sum_{j=1}^{k}\frac{\sigma^2}{d_j},
$$

which is unbounded as any $d_j \to 0$: the estimator is unbiased in every direction
and hopeless in the ones the design barely spans. Consider instead the family of
shrinkage estimators $\hat\beta(\lambda) = (X^\top X + \lambda I_k)^{-1}X^\top y$,
which is least squares at $\lambda = 0$. Its mean squared error is

$$
\text{MSE}(\lambda) = \sum_{j=1}^{k}\frac{\lambda^2\gamma_j^2 + d_j\sigma^2}{(d_j+\lambda)^2},
\qquad
\text{MSE}'(0) = -\sum_{j=1}^{k}\frac{2\sigma^2}{d_j^2} \;<\; 0 ,
$$

for every $\beta$, every $\sigma^2 > 0$ and every design. Some shrinkage strictly
improves on least squares no matter what the truth is, and the improvement is largest
exactly where $d_j$ is smallest.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Work in the eigenbasis, which loses no generality and makes every matrix diagonal.
Since $\hat\beta_{\text{OLS}} \sim \mathcal{N}(\beta, \sigma^2(X^\top X)^{-1})$ and $Q$
is orthogonal, the rotated estimate $\hat\gamma = Q^\top\hat\beta_{\text{OLS}}$
satisfies

$$
\hat\gamma_j \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\gamma_j, \; \frac{\sigma^2}{d_j}\right),
\qquad j = 1, \dots, k,
$$

independently across $j$, because $Q^\top(X^\top X)^{-1}Q = D^{-1}$ is diagonal.
Orthogonal maps preserve length, so
$\|\hat\beta_{\text{OLS}} - \beta\|^2 = \|\hat\gamma - \gamma\|^2$ and its expectation
is $\sum_j \sigma^2/d_j$, the first display.

For the shrinkage family, $(X^\top X + \lambda I_k)^{-1}X^\top y = Q(D+\lambda
I_k)^{-1}DQ^\top\hat\beta_{\text{OLS}}$, so in the rotated coordinates the estimator is
the coordinate-wise scaling $w_j\hat\gamma_j$ with $w_j = d_j/(d_j+\lambda)$. Its
expectation is $w_j\gamma_j$, so the bias is

$$
\text{bias}_j = -(1-w_j)\gamma_j = -\frac{\lambda}{d_j+\lambda}\gamma_j ,
$$

zero at $\lambda = 0$ and tending to $-\gamma_j$ as $\lambda \to \infty$: an infinitely
tight prior reports zero and is wrong by the whole coefficient. Its variance is
$w_j^2\sigma^2/d_j = d_j\sigma^2/(d_j+\lambda)^2$, starting at the least-squares value
$\sigma^2/d_j$ and falling monotonically to zero. Adding squared bias to variance and
summing gives the displayed $\text{MSE}(\lambda)$. At $\lambda = 0$ it is
$\sum_j\sigma^2/d_j$, pure variance; as $\lambda\to\infty$ it tends to
$\sum_j\gamma_j^2$, pure squared bias.

Differentiating one term, with
$f_j(\lambda) = (\lambda^2\gamma_j^2 + d_j\sigma^2)/(d_j+\lambda)^2$,

$$
f_j'(\lambda)
= \frac{2\lambda\gamma_j^2(d_j+\lambda)^2 - 2(d_j+\lambda)(\lambda^2\gamma_j^2 + d_j\sigma^2)}{(d_j+\lambda)^4}
= \frac{2d_j\left(\lambda\gamma_j^2 - \sigma^2\right)}{(d_j+\lambda)^3},
$$

after expanding and cancelling the $\lambda^2\gamma_j^2$ terms. Setting $\lambda = 0$
gives $f_j'(0) = -2\sigma^2/d_j^2 < 0$ in every coordinate, which is the second display.
Two further consequences follow. The coordinate-wise optimum is
$\lambda_j^\ast = \sigma^2/\gamma_j^2$, the noise variance divided by the squared true
coefficient, so a prior whose variance matches the dispersion of the coefficients one
actually expects is the one that minimises mean squared error. And because a single
$\lambda$ must serve every coordinate, the practical optimum solves
$\sum_j 2d_j(\lambda\gamma_j^2-\sigma^2)/(d_j+\lambda)^3 = 0$, a weighted average of the
coordinate-wise optima with weights $d_j/(d_j+\lambda)^3$, in which the poorly measured
directions carry the largest weight.
:::

The result is a statement about the design matrix, so it can be checked on the design
matrix. The chunk below takes the $37 \times 37$ cross-product matrix of the estimation
window and reads off its eigenvalues.

```{python}
d_eig = np.linalg.eigvalsh(X_var.T @ X_var)[::-1]
var_dir = sig2_in[0] / d_eig                       # sigma^2 / d_j, output equation
lam_show = [0.0, 1.0, 10.0, 100.0]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 4.0))
axes[0].semilogy(np.arange(1, k_var + 1), d_eig, "o-", ms=4)
axes[0].set_xlabel("eigenvalue rank $j$"); axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$d_j$")
axes[0].set_title("Eigenvalues of $X^\\top X$, twelve-lag monthly VAR")
for lam in lam_show:
    axes[1].plot(np.arange(1, k_var + 1), d_eig / (d_eig + lam), "-o", ms=3,
                 label=rf"$\lambda = {lam:g}$")
axes[1].set_xlabel("eigenvalue rank $j$"); axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$d_j/(d_j+\lambda)$")
axes[1].set_title("Weight kept on the data, by direction"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"largest eigenvalue {d_eig[0]:.4g}, smallest {d_eig[-1]:.4g}, "
      f"condition number {d_eig[0] / d_eig[-1]:.4g}")
print(f"sum of sigma^2/d_j, output equation: {var_dir.sum():.4f}")
print(f"squared length of the least-squares estimate: "
      f"{np.sum(B_ols_var[:, 0] ** 2):.4f}")
print(f"share of that variance from the five worst directions: "
      f"{var_dir[-5:].sum() / var_dir.sum():.4f}")
```

The left panel is the diagnosis. The eigenvalues span five orders of magnitude, from
$4.528 \times 10^{4}$ down to $0.2231$, a condition number of $2.029 \times 10^{5}$.
Twelve lags of three persistent series are very nearly linear combinations of one
another, so the design is close to singular in many directions at once, and those are
precisely the directions in which R-6.1 says the variance explodes. Summing
$\sigma^2/d_j$ over all thirty-seven directions gives $6.2159$ for the output equation
against a squared length of the estimate itself of $7.6116$: the expected squared error
of least squares is four fifths as large as the entire quantity being estimated, and
$57.6$ percent of that error comes from the five worst-measured directions alone, which
are five of thirty-seven.

The right panel is the repair in outline. The factor $d_j/(d_j+\lambda)$ is what a
Normal prior keeps of the data in each direction. It is essentially one in the
well-measured directions at the left of the picture, so a prior costs almost nothing
there, and it falls towards zero in exactly the directions where $\sigma^2/d_j$ is
largest. A prior does not shrink a coefficient because the coefficient is small. It
shrinks a direction because the sample cannot see it.

Two things remain to be settled, and they occupy the next section. The first is what
$W$ looks like for a general prior rather than the single scalar $\lambda$ used here.
The second, and the one with the economics in it, is how to choose $B_0$ for a
vector autoregression so that the directions the prior tightens are the ones a
macroeconomist would be willing to tighten.

## Methodology: a structured Normal prior on the lag coefficients {#sec-methodology}

The repair is to give $\beta$ a proper prior, which converts the ill-posed estimation
problem into a well-posed one by supplying information where the sample has none. The
first result says what any Normal prior does. The second says what to put in it.

### Result R-6.2: the posterior mean as a shrinkage matrix

For $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2 I_n)$ and
$\beta \sim \mathcal{N}(b_0, B_0)$ with $B_0$ positive definite, the posterior is exactly
Normal,

$$
\beta \mid y \sim \mathcal{N}(m, V),
\qquad
V = \left(\frac{X^\top X}{\sigma^2} + B_0^{-1}\right)^{-1},
\qquad
m = V\left(\frac{X^\top y}{\sigma^2} + B_0^{-1}b_0\right),
$$

for any $n$, any $k$ and any $X$, invertible $X^\top X$ or not. Whenever $X^\top X$ is
invertible the mean can be rewritten as a matrix-weighted average,

$$
m = W\hat\beta_{\text{OLS}} + (I_k - W)\,b_0,
\qquad
W = \left(\frac{X^\top X}{\sigma^2} + B_0^{-1}\right)^{-1}\frac{X^\top X}{\sigma^2},
$$

and every eigenvalue of $W$ lies strictly in $(0,1)$. With the isotropic prior
$B_0 = \tau^2 I_k$ this collapses to $m = (X^\top X + \lambda I_k)^{-1}X^\top y$ with
$\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2$, which is the ridge estimator, so ridge regression is not a
rival to the Bayesian treatment but the special case of it in which every direction is
given the same prior variance.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Drop every term free of $\beta$ from the log posterior,

$$
\log p(\beta \mid y) = -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(y - X\beta)^\top(y - X\beta)
-\frac{1}{2}(\beta - b_0)^\top B_0^{-1}(\beta - b_0) + \text{const},
$$

expand both quadratics and collect by the power of $\beta$. The quadratic terms are

$$
-\frac{1}{2}\beta^\top\left(\frac{X^\top X}{\sigma^2} + B_0^{-1}\right)\beta
\equiv -\frac{1}{2}\beta^\top V^{-1}\beta,
$$

and the linear terms are $\beta^\top(X^\top y/\sigma^2 + B_0^{-1}b_0)$. A Normal density
with mean $m$ and covariance $V$ has log kernel
$-\tfrac12\beta^\top V^{-1}\beta + \beta^\top V^{-1}m$, so matching the linear terms
gives $V^{-1}m = X^\top y/\sigma^2 + B_0^{-1}b_0$ and hence the displayed $m$. No other
power of $\beta$ appears, so the posterior is exactly Normal and these two moments
describe it completely.

For the weighted-average form, substitute $X^\top y = X^\top X\hat\beta_{\text{OLS}}$,

$$
m = V\left(\frac{X^\top X}{\sigma^2}\hat\beta_{\text{OLS}} + B_0^{-1}b_0\right)
= W\hat\beta_{\text{OLS}} + VB_0^{-1}b_0 ,
$$

and note that $VB_0^{-1} = V(V^{-1} - X^\top X/\sigma^2) = I_k - W$, which gives the
second display. For the eigenvalues, take $B_0 = \tau^2 I_k$ and write $X^\top X =
QDQ^\top$, so that

$$
W = Q\left(D + \lambda I_k\right)^{-1}D\,Q^\top
= Q\operatorname{diag}\!\left(\frac{d_j}{d_j+\lambda}\right)Q^\top,
\qquad \lambda = \frac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2},
$$

each factor lying strictly in $(0,1)$ for $\lambda > 0$, and the smallest $d_j$ giving
the smallest factor: the direction the data see worst is shrunk hardest, which is R-6.1
answered. For general $B_0$ the same statement holds in the metric of $B_0$, since $W$
is a product of two positive definite matrices and is therefore similar to
$V^{1/2}(X^\top X/\sigma^2)V^{1/2}$, whose eigenvalues lie in $(0,1)$ because
$V^{-1}$ exceeds $X^\top X/\sigma^2$ in the positive definite order.

Two limits are worth recording. As $B_0^{-1}\to 0$ the prior becomes flat, $W \to I_k$,
and the posterior mean is least squares. As $B_0^{-1}\to\infty$ the prior dominates,
$W \to 0$, and the posterior mean is $b_0$. The matrix $W$ is not a scalar multiple of
the identity unless $X^\top X$ and $B_0^{-1}$ are simultaneously isotropic, which is
why shrinking every coefficient by a common fraction is in general the wrong operation.
Finally, in the scaled parameterisation of this course,
$\beta \mid \sigma^2 \sim \mathcal{N}(b_0, \sigma^2 B_0)$ with
$\sigma^2 \sim \text{IG}(\alpha_0,\delta_0)$, the factor $\sigma^2$ cancels from both
terms and $m = (X^\top X + B_0^{-1})^{-1}(X^\top y + B_0^{-1}b_0)$, which is why that
version locates the posterior mean without any estimate of $\sigma^2$.
:::

Result R-6.2 is a machine with a slot in it. Everything economic lives in $B_0$, and
nothing so far says what to put there. For a vector autoregression the answer is the
Minnesota prior, introduced by Litterman and his coauthors at the Minneapolis Fed,
which builds $B_0$ out of three statements a macroeconomist is willing to sign.

### Result R-6.3: the Minnesota prior variance

Write the system as $y_{it} = c_i + \sum_{\ell=1}^{p}\sum_{j=1}^{m}A_{ij\ell}\,
y_{j,t-\ell} + u_{it}$ and let $\sigma_i$ denote the scale of variable $i$, measured by
its residual standard deviation. The Minnesota prior is the independent Normal prior
with mean

$$
\mathbb{E}[A_{ij\ell}] = \delta_i\,\mathbb{1}\{i = j,\; \ell = 1\},
$$

a diffuse prior on each intercept, and variance

$$
\operatorname{Var}(A_{ij\ell}) =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\lambda_1}{\ell^{2}}, & i = j,\\[2ex]
\dfrac{\lambda_1\lambda_2}{\ell^{2}}\,\dfrac{\sigma_i^2}{\sigma_j^2}, & i \neq j,
\end{cases}
$$

with $\lambda_1 > 0$ the overall tightness and $\lambda_2 \in (0,1)$ the extra shrinkage
applied to cross lags. The whole prior covariance of a system of any size is fixed by
two numbers. The prior is invariant to the units of every variable, the total prior
variance it attributes to the lag structure converges as $p$ grows, and the entire
matrix $B_0$ is diagonal, so R-6.2 applies to it directly.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Each of the three ingredients follows from one statement.

Units. The coefficient $A_{ij\ell}$ multiplies variable $j$ and contributes to
variable $i$, so it carries the units of $y_i$ per unit of $y_j$. A claim of the form
"this coefficient is probably no larger than $0.2$" is therefore meaningless until the
units are fixed: quoting $y_j$ in basis points instead of percent multiplies the same
economic relation by one hundred. Make the claim dimensionless instead. Define the
standardised coefficient $\tilde A_{ij\ell} = A_{ij\ell}\sigma_j/\sigma_i$, which
answers how many standard deviations of $y_i$ move when $y_j$ moves by one of its own.
A belief $\operatorname{Var}(\tilde A_{ij\ell}) = \kappa_{ij\ell}$ for a dimensionless
$\kappa$ translates back into

$$
\operatorname{Var}(A_{ij\ell}) = \kappa_{ij\ell}\,\frac{\sigma_i^2}{\sigma_j^2},
$$

which is where the scale ratio comes from. It is not a correction bolted on afterwards;
it is what makes $\kappa$ mean the same thing in every cell. For an own lag, $i = j$,
the ratio is exactly one, which is why it is absent from the own-lag line rather than
treated differently there. The formal content is invariance: rescaling
$\tilde y_j = c\,y_j$ divides the coefficient by $c$ to leave the equation unchanged and
multiplies $\sigma_j$ by $c$, so the prior standard deviation
$\sqrt{\kappa}\,\sigma_i/\sigma_j$ is divided by $c$ as well, and the belief is
untouched. Without the ratio a harmless change of units would silently retighten the
prior.

Lag decay. If the coefficient at lag $\ell$ has prior standard deviation $s_\ell$, the
term $A_{ij\ell}y_{j,t-\ell}$ contributes prior variance of order
$s_\ell^2\sigma_j^2$ to the fitted value, so the lag structure as a whole contributes
of order $\sigma_j^2\sum_\ell s_\ell^2$. For that sum to converge as more lags are
added, so that lengthening $p$ does not keep inflating the implied variability of the
fitted value, $s_\ell^2$ must be summable. The choice $s_\ell \propto 1/\ell$ is the
simplest summable sequence of the right qualitative shape, and gives
$\sum_{\ell\ge1}1/\ell^2 = \pi^2/6 \approx 1.645$, so the entire lag structure beyond
the first contributes less prior variability than the first lag alone. Adding lags to a
Minnesota system is therefore close to free, which is the property that lets twelve
monthly lags be used where least squares is hopeless. Writing $\lambda_1$ for the
variance at $\ell = 1$ gives $\kappa_{ij\ell} = \lambda_1/\ell^2$ up to the own-cross
distinction.

Own lags against cross lags. Two arguments point the same way. The first is about the
benchmark. The prior mean is a set of univariate random walks, in which a variable's own
first lag enters with coefficient one and nothing else enters at all, so the own first
lag is the only coefficient whose prior mean is non-zero. A tight prior around zero for
a cross lag says that a channel probably is not there, which is a modest claim; a
tight prior around one for an own lag would say that a variable is exactly a random
walk, which is a far stronger one. Loosening own lags and tightening cross lags is the
only assignment consistent with being confident about the absences and agnostic about
the persistence. The second argument is about where the sample is informative. A
macroeconomic series is strongly autocorrelated, so its own lags are measured relatively
precisely, while information about a cross lag must be extracted from the part of $y_j$
not already explained by $y_i$'s own history, which in a persistent system is small. By
R-6.2 the weight kept on the data is increasing in the sample precision, so a common
prior variance would leave the well-measured own lags almost untouched and shrink the
badly measured cross lags only moderately, and the estimator would still inherit most of
the noise. The factor $\lambda_2 \in (0,1)$ puts the shrinkage where the sample is
silent.

Prior mean and intercept. The benchmark makes no claim about the level of a series, so
shrinking an intercept towards zero would pull the variable towards zero rather than
towards a random walk, which is the opposite of the intended belief; the intercept
therefore gets a near-diffuse variance $\lambda_c$. The own-first-lag prior mean
$\delta_i$ is one for a variable modelled in levels and zero for a variable already
differenced, because for a growth rate the random-walk belief about the underlying level
is precisely the statement that the growth rate has no predictable own dynamics.

Combining the three gives the displayed variance, with each factor traceable to a
statement about units, about summability across lags, or about where the sample is
informative. Since $B_0$ is diagonal, the posterior mean of R-6.2 can be formed
directly, and since the prior variance differs across the elements of the coefficient
matrix it cannot be written as a Kronecker product of a coefficient covariance with the
error covariance. The Minnesota specification is therefore not conjugate for the full
system, which is why the system posterior of Lecture 7 needs a two-block sampler rather
than a closed form; conditional on a fixed error covariance, which is what this chapter
uses, R-6.2 gives the answer exactly.
:::

One property of R-6.3 deserves stating outside the callout, because it is what makes
the prior usable rather than merely defensible. Two numbers, $\lambda_1$ and
$\lambda_2$, specify the prior variance of every coefficient in a system of any size.
There is nothing to elicit coefficient by coefficient, no expert judgement about the
ninth lag of inflation in the output equation, and no scope for the prior to be tuned
until the answer looks right. What is left to choose, $\lambda_1$, is a single dial
whose consequences can be measured on forecasts, which is what @sec-empirical does.

## Data: output, prices and the policy rate, 1960 to 2026 {#sec-data}

The chapter's dataset is the monthly FRED macroeconomic snapshot,
`data/fred_macro_monthly.parquet`, and the three series used are industrial production,
the consumer price index and the effective federal funds rate. They describe activity,
prices and the policy stance, which are the three blocks every small monetary model
contains, and they are the only series used anywhere in this chapter.

The two index levels are transformed before they enter the system, because both trend
upwards without bound and a regression of one trend on another describes nothing. We
use one hundred times the monthly log difference, so a value of $0.3$ reads as growth of
three tenths of a percent in that month. The funds rate enters in percentage points,
since a policy rate has no trend to remove and its level is what policy makers choose.

```{python}
#| label: fig-macro-panel
#| fig-cap: "The three series of the chapter over the whole snapshot, with the 1990s estimation window shaded. Output growth and inflation are monthly log changes in percent; the funds rate is in percentage points."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(7.5, 6.4), sharex=True)
for ax, nm, lab in zip(axes, var_names,
                       ["IP growth (% per month)", "CPI inflation (% per month)",
                        "federal funds rate (%)"]):
    ax.plot(mac.index, mac[nm], lw=0.7, color="steelblue")
    ax.axvspan(pd.Timestamp(est_start), pd.Timestamp(est_end), color="grey", alpha=0.25)
    ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.6)
    ax.set_ylabel(lab, fontsize=9)
axes[0].set_title("Output, prices and the policy rate, 1960-2026")
axes[-1].set_xlabel("date")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"{len(mac)} months, {mac.index[0]:%Y-%m} to {mac.index[-1]:%Y-%m}")
print(mac.describe().loc[["mean", "std", "min", "max"]].round(3).to_string())
print(f"window standard deviations, {est_start} to {est_end}: "
      f"{np.round(mac.loc[est_start:est_end].std().to_numpy(), 3)}")
```

The transformed panel runs from February 1960 to July 2026, $796$ months. Industrial
production grows by $0.183$ percent a month on average with a standard deviation of
$0.948$, and its minimum of $-14.142$ percent is April 2020, a single observation an
order of magnitude beyond anything else in the sample. Inflation averages $0.305$
percent a month, which compounds to about $3.7$ percent a year, with a standard
deviation of $0.313$ and a minimum of $-1.786$ percent in November 2008. The funds rate
averages $4.783$ percent and ranges from $0.05$ to $19.1$, the upper end being the
Volcker disinflation of 1981.

The three panels also explain the estimation window. A twelve-lag linear model fitted
across a series that reaches nineteen percent in 1981 and sits at essentially zero from
2009 to 2015 is describing an average of several different monetary policies rather than
one. Inside the shaded window output growth is visibly calmer, with a standard deviation
of $0.526$ against $0.948$ over the whole sample. That is the choice @sec-motivation
made and it is the source of its difficulty: a homogeneous decade is exactly $120$
observations.

## Empirical analysis: shrinking a twelve-lag monthly VAR {#sec-empirical}

### The prior, in numbers

We build the prior of R-6.3 for this system, taking $\lambda_1 = 0.05$ and
$\lambda_2 = 0.5$ for the first pass and $\lambda_c = 100$ for the intercepts, and using
the sample standard deviations of the window for the scale ratios. The prior mean vector
on own first lags is $(0,0,1)$, zero for the two differenced series and one for the
funds rate, exactly as the last paragraph of the R-6.3 derivation requires.

```{python}
#| label: fig-prior-structure
#| fig-cap: "The Minnesota prior standard deviation for every lag coefficient of the three-variable, twelve-lag system. Rows are equations, columns are the thirty-six lagged regressors in the order lag one variable one, lag one variable two, and so on."
def minn_prior_pieces(m, p, sig, lam1, lam2, lam_c, rw_mean):
    k = 1 + m * p
    B0, V = np.zeros((k, m)), np.zeros((k, m))
    V[0, :] = lam_c                                    # near-diffuse intercept
    for ell in range(1, p + 1):
        for j in range(m):                             # regressor: lag ell of variable j
            row = 1 + (ell - 1) * m + j
            for i in range(m):                         # equation for variable i
                V[row, i] = (lam1 / ell**2 if i == j else
                             lam1 * lam2 / ell**2 * sig[i]**2 / sig[j]**2)
            if ell == 1:
                B0[row, j] = rw_mean[j]
    return B0, V

def minn_post_mean(X, Y, Sigma, sig, lam1, lam2=0.5, lam_c=100.0,
                   rw_mean=(0.0, 0.0, 1.0), p=12):
    k, m = X.shape[1], Y.shape[1]
    B0, V = minn_prior_pieces(m, p, sig, lam1, lam2, lam_c, np.asarray(rw_mean))
    inv_sigma = np.linalg.inv(Sigma)
    prec0 = np.diag(1.0 / V.ravel(order="F"))
    Vfull = np.linalg.inv(prec0 + np.kron(inv_sigma, X.T @ X))
    b = Vfull @ (prec0 @ B0.ravel(order="F") + (X.T @ Y @ inv_sigma).ravel(order="F"))
    return b.reshape(k, m, order="F")

sig_var = win.std(axis=0, ddof=1)
lam1_var, lam2_var = 0.05, 0.5
B0_var, V0_var = minn_prior_pieces(m_var, p_var, sig_var, lam1_var, lam2_var,
                                   100.0, np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 3.2))
im = ax.imshow(np.sqrt(V0_var[1:].T), aspect="auto", cmap="viridis")
ax.set_yticks(range(m_var)); ax.set_yticklabels([f"eq. {nm}" for nm in var_names],
                                                fontsize=8)
ax.set_xticks(np.arange(0, m_var * p_var, m_var))
ax.set_xticklabels([f"L{ell}" for ell in range(1, p_var + 1)], fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlabel("lag block (three regressors each)")
ax.set_title("Minnesota prior standard deviation by coefficient")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="prior sd")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"scale standard deviations used for the ratios: {np.round(sig_var, 4)}")
print(f"own-lag prior sd: lag 1 {np.sqrt(lam1_var):.4f}, "
      f"lag 12 {np.sqrt(lam1_var) / p_var:.4f}")
for (i, j) in [(0, 2), (2, 0)]:
    print(f"cross-lag prior sd, equation {var_names[i]} on {var_names[j]}, lag 1: "
          f"{np.sqrt(lam1_var * lam2_var) * sig_var[i] / sig_var[j]:.4f}")
```

The picture is R-6.3 drawn. The three bright cells in each lag block are the own lags,
which carry a prior standard deviation of $\sqrt{\lambda_1}/\ell$, that is $0.2236$ at
lag one and $0.0186$ at lag twelve. Everything else is a cross lag, dimmer by the factor
$\sqrt{\lambda_2}$ and then rescaled by $\sigma_i/\sigma_j$. That rescaling is large
here: the prior standard deviation on the funds rate's lag in the output equation is
$0.0469$, while the one on output's lag in the funds rate equation is $0.5334$, a ratio
of more than eleven, because the funds rate is more than eleven times as volatile as
output growth in this window. A single number $\sqrt{\lambda_1\lambda_2} = 0.1581$
expresses the same belief in both cells once the units are divided out, and would
express two wildly different beliefs if they were not.

### What the prior does to the coefficients

```{python}
#| label: fig-ols-vs-minnesota
#| fig-cap: "The 108 lag coefficients of the twelve-lag monthly VAR, least squares against the Minnesota posterior mean. The left panel orders them by lag, the right panel plots one against the other."
resid_var = Y_var - X_var @ B_ols_var
Sigma_ols_var = resid_var.T @ resid_var / (X_var.shape[0] - k_var)
B_minn_var = minn_post_mean(X_var, Y_var, Sigma_ols_var, sig_var, lam1_var, lam2_var)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 4.2))
jitter = np.linspace(-0.28, 0.28, m_var)
for eq in range(m_var):
    axes[0].plot(lag_index + jitter[eq], B_ols_var[1:, eq], "o", ms=3.2, alpha=0.55,
                 color="grey", label="least squares" if eq == 0 else None)
    axes[0].plot(lag_index + jitter[eq], B_minn_var[1:, eq], "s", ms=3.2, alpha=0.8,
                 color="firebrick", label="Minnesota posterior mean" if eq == 0 else None)
axes[0].axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
axes[0].set_xlabel("lag"); axes[0].set_ylabel("coefficient")
axes[0].set_title("Coefficients by lag"); axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)

lims = [min(B_ols_var[1:].min(), B_minn_var[1:].min()) - 0.1,
        max(B_ols_var[1:].max(), B_minn_var[1:].max()) + 0.1]
axes[1].plot(lims, lims, "k--", lw=1, label="45 degree line")
axes[1].axhline(0, color="grey", lw=0.6); axes[1].axvline(0, color="grey", lw=0.6)
axes[1].scatter(B_ols_var[1:].ravel(), B_minn_var[1:].ravel(), s=14, alpha=0.7)
axes[1].set_xlabel("least-squares coefficient"); axes[1].set_ylabel("posterior mean")
axes[1].set_title("Shrinkage across all 108 lag coefficients"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"largest |lag coefficient|: OLS {np.abs(B_ols_var[1:]).max():.3f}, "
      f"Minnesota {np.abs(B_minn_var[1:]).max():.3f}")
print(f"sum of |lag coefficients|: OLS {np.abs(B_ols_var[1:]).sum():.3f}, "
      f"Minnesota {np.abs(B_minn_var[1:]).sum():.3f}")
print(f"std dev across lag coefficients: OLS {B_ols_var[1:].std():.4f}, "
      f"Minnesota {B_minn_var[1:].std():.4f}")
print(f"mean |Minnesota - OLS|: {np.abs(B_minn_var[1:] - B_ols_var[1:]).mean():.4f}, "
      f"largest {np.abs(B_minn_var[1:] - B_ols_var[1:]).max():.4f}")
print(f"share of lag coefficients closer to zero: "
      f"{np.mean(np.abs(B_minn_var[1:]) < np.abs(B_ols_var[1:])):.3f}")
```

The two fits describe very different systems. Least squares spreads a total absolute
coefficient mass of $18.644$ across the $108$ lag coefficients; the posterior mean
spreads $4.334$. The dispersion across coefficients falls from $0.3071$ to $0.1274$, and
$88.0$ percent of the lag coefficients end up smaller in absolute value than their
least-squares counterparts, with the average coefficient moving by $0.1424$ and the
largest by $1.5881$. That largest move is the $-1.598$ coefficient from
@sec-motivation, which is now essentially gone. The largest surviving entry is $1.148$,
the funds rate's own first lag sitting just above its prior mean of one, which is a
coefficient nobody would call implausible.

The left panel shows the mechanism and the right panel the summary. Least squares
scatters coefficients of either sign across all twelve lags with no decline in magnitude,
which is what fitting noise looks like; the Minnesota points sit in a band around zero
that narrows with the lag, the $1/\ell^2$ decay of R-6.3 made visible. In the right panel
the cloud lies systematically inside the forty-five degree line, and the few points near
it are the coefficients the sample genuinely pins down, mostly short own lags. Nothing in
the data changed between the two fits. Only the willingness to believe that a
coefficient on the ninth lag of inflation is genuinely large.

```{python}
def companion_matrix(B, m, p):
    C = np.zeros((m * p, m * p))
    for ell in range(p):
        C[:m, ell * m:(ell + 1) * m] = B[1 + ell * m: 1 + (ell + 1) * m, :].T
    if p > 1:
        C[m:, :m * (p - 1)] = np.eye(m * (p - 1))
    return C

eig_ols = np.abs(np.linalg.eigvals(companion_matrix(B_ols_var, m_var, p_var))).max()
eig_minn = np.abs(np.linalg.eigvals(companion_matrix(B_minn_var, m_var, p_var))).max()
print(f"largest companion eigenvalue modulus: OLS {eig_ols:.4f}, "
      f"Minnesota {eig_minn:.4f}")
print(f"implied half-life of a shock, months: OLS {np.log(0.5)/np.log(eig_ols):.1f}, "
      f"Minnesota {np.log(0.5)/np.log(eig_minn):.1f}")
```

Both systems are stable, but the least-squares one sits closer to the unit circle at
$0.9623$ against $0.9300$. That difference sounds small and is not: the implied half-life
of a shock falls from $18.0$ months to $9.6$. Over a twelve-month horizon the two models
therefore extrapolate the last observed year very differently, which is the mechanism
behind everything that follows. The eigenvalue is also the summary statistic to watch when
the tightness is chosen, because it is the one number that says whether a fitted system
will produce sensible iterated forecasts at all: a companion root above one implies paths
that diverge, and unrestricted least squares on a short window crosses that line regularly
once the lag length or the number of variables rises even slightly above the setting used
here.

### Does it forecast better?

Coefficients are not the object of interest, forecasts are, so the tightness is chosen
by measuring its consequences rather than by assertion. The experiment is an
expanding-window pseudo out-of-sample comparison. The estimation sample always starts in
January 1990. For each forecast origin from December 1999 to the end of the data the
system is estimated on everything available up to that month, iterated forward twelve
months, and scored against what actually happened. Nothing after the origin ever enters
the estimation. Three benchmarks share the same origins: the random walk, which predicts
no change; an AR(1) for each variable, re-estimated at every origin; and the same
twelve-lag system fitted by least squares.

```{python}
def var_forecast_path(B, hist, H):
    out = np.zeros((H, B.shape[1]))
    window = hist.copy()                            # (p, m), newest row first
    for h in range(H):
        ynew = np.concatenate([[1.0], window.ravel()]) @ B
        out[h] = ynew
        window = np.vstack([ynew, window[:-1]])
    return out

H_var = 12
origins = [d for d in mac.index
           if pd.Timestamp("1999-12-01") <= d <= mac.index[-1] - pd.DateOffset(months=1)]
lam_grid = [0.001, 0.002, 0.005, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1.0]
models = ["ols", "rw", "ar1"] + [f"minn{lam:g}" for lam in lam_grid]
err = {(mod, h): [] for mod in models for h in range(1, H_var + 1)}

for origin in origins:
    D = mac.loc["1990-01":origin].to_numpy()
    Xo, Yo = build_var_xy(D, p_var)
    sig_o = D.std(axis=0, ddof=1)
    B_o = np.linalg.solve(Xo.T @ Xo, Xo.T @ Yo)
    r_o = Yo - Xo @ B_o
    Sig_o = r_o.T @ r_o / (Xo.shape[0] - Xo.shape[1])
    hist = D[-p_var:][::-1]
    future = mac.loc[origin + pd.DateOffset(months=1):
                     origin + pd.DateOffset(months=H_var)].to_numpy()

    paths = {"ols": var_forecast_path(B_o, hist, H_var),
             "rw": np.tile(D[-1], (H_var, 1))}
    for lam in lam_grid:
        paths[f"minn{lam:g}"] = var_forecast_path(
            minn_post_mean(Xo, Yo, Sig_o, sig_o, lam), hist, H_var)
    ar = np.array([np.linalg.solve(
        np.column_stack([np.ones(len(D) - 1), D[:-1, i]]).T
        @ np.column_stack([np.ones(len(D) - 1), D[:-1, i]]),
        np.column_stack([np.ones(len(D) - 1), D[:-1, i]]).T @ D[1:, i])
        for i in range(m_var)])
    ar_path = np.zeros((H_var, m_var)); cur = D[-1].copy()
    for h in range(H_var):
        cur = ar[:, 0] + ar[:, 1] * cur
        ar_path[h] = cur
    paths["ar1"] = ar_path

    for mod, path in paths.items():
        for h in range(1, future.shape[0] + 1):
            err[(mod, h)].append(path[h - 1] - future[h - 1])

def rmsfe(mod, idx=None):
    return np.array([np.sqrt(np.mean(np.array(err[(mod, h)])[slice(None) if idx is None
                                                             else idx] ** 2, axis=0))
                     for h in range(1, H_var + 1)])

print(f"{len(origins)} forecast origins, {origins[0]:%Y-%m} to {origins[-1]:%Y-%m}")
print(f"usable observations at the first origin "
      f"{len(mac.loc['1990-01':origins[0]]) - p_var}, at the last "
      f"{len(mac.loc['1990-01':origins[-1]]) - p_var}")
print(f"one-month-ahead errors {len(err[('ols', 1)])}, "
      f"twelve-month-ahead errors {len(err[('ols', 12)])}")
```

Three hundred and seventeen origins, from December 1999 to June 2026, give $317$
one-month-ahead errors and $298$ twelve-month-ahead errors, the difference being the
horizons that run past the end of the sample. The parameter count stays at $111$
throughout while the usable observations grow from $108$ at the first origin to $424$ at
the last, so the experiment also records how the value of shrinkage decays as data
accumulate.

```{python}
#| label: fig-tightness-sweep
#| fig-cap: "One-month-ahead root mean squared forecast error as a function of the overall Minnesota tightness, each variable scaled by the random-walk benchmark. The dashed line of matching colour is the unrestricted VAR for the same variable."
rmsfe_rw, rmsfe_ols = rmsfe("rw"), rmsfe("ols")
curves = {lam: rmsfe(f"minn{lam:g}") for lam in lam_grid}

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for i, nm in enumerate(var_names):
    ax.plot(lam_grid, [curves[lam][0, i] / rmsfe_rw[0, i] for lam in lam_grid],
            "-o", ms=4, color=f"C{i}", label=nm)
    ax.axhline(rmsfe_ols[0, i] / rmsfe_rw[0, i], color=f"C{i}", ls="--", lw=1)
ax.axhline(1.0, color="black", lw=1, label="random walk")
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel(r"overall tightness $\lambda_1$  (looser $\to$)")
ax.set_ylabel("RMSFE relative to the random walk, h = 1")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Forecast accuracy against prior tightness, one month ahead")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("best lambda_1 at h = 1 by variable:",
      {nm: lam_grid[int(np.argmin([curves[lam][0, i] for lam in lam_grid]))]
       for i, nm in enumerate(var_names)})
for i, nm in enumerate(var_names):
    print(f"{nm}: h=1 RMSFE relative to the random walk, OLS "
          f"{rmsfe_ols[0, i] / rmsfe_rw[0, i]:.3f}, best Minnesota "
          f"{min(curves[lam][0, i] for lam in lam_grid) / rmsfe_rw[0, i]:.3f}")
```

Every Minnesota curve lies below its own dashed least-squares line at every tightness on
the grid, which is the first result: on this panel there is no value of $\lambda_1$ so
loose that shrinkage hurts relative to the unrestricted system. The curves are not
monotone in the same direction, and the differences are economically legible. Inflation
is best forecast at $\lambda_1 = 0.03$ and the funds rate at $0.005$, both interior
minima, so for those two there is a genuine trade-off and over-shrinking eventually
costs accuracy, exactly as the U-shape of R-6.1 predicts. Output growth keeps improving
as the prior tightens all the way to $0.001$, because monthly industrial production
growth is close to unforecastable one month ahead and a prior that shrinks everything
nearly to zero is very close to the right model. The dashed lines record how badly the
unrestricted system does on inflation in particular, where it barely improves on the
random walk at all, a ratio of $0.997$ against $0.889$ at the best tightness.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rmsfe-by-horizon
#| fig-cap: "Root mean squared forecast error by horizon for the three variables, over 317 expanding-window origins from December 1999. Lower is better."
lam_show = 0.03
rmsfe_minn, rmsfe_ar1 = rmsfe(f"minn{lam_show:g}"), rmsfe("ar1")
hgrid = np.arange(1, H_var + 1)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.8))
for i, (ax, nm) in enumerate(zip(axes, var_names)):
    ax.plot(hgrid, rmsfe_ols[:, i], "-o", ms=3, color="grey", label="OLS VAR")
    ax.plot(hgrid, rmsfe_minn[:, i], "-s", ms=3, color="firebrick",
            label=rf"Minnesota $\lambda_1={lam_show}$")
    ax.plot(hgrid, rmsfe_rw[:, i], "-^", ms=3, color="steelblue", label="random walk")
    ax.plot(hgrid, rmsfe_ar1[:, i], "-v", ms=3, color="seagreen", label="AR(1)")
    ax.set_xlabel("horizon (months)"); ax.set_title(nm, fontsize=10)
    if i == 0:
        ax.set_ylabel("RMSFE"); ax.legend(fontsize=7)
fig.suptitle("Out-of-sample forecast accuracy, 317 expanding-window origins")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

tab = pd.DataFrame(index=[f"h={h}" for h in (1, 3, 6, 12)])
for nm_mod, R in [("OLS VAR", rmsfe_ols), ("Minnesota", rmsfe_minn),
                  ("random walk", rmsfe_rw), ("AR(1)", rmsfe_ar1)]:
    for i, nm in enumerate(var_names):
        tab[f"{nm_mod}: {nm}"] = [R[h - 1, i] for h in (1, 3, 6, 12)]
print(tab.T.round(4).to_string())
ratio = rmsfe_minn / rmsfe_ols
print(f"\nMinnesota beats OLS in {int((ratio < 1).sum())} of {ratio.size} "
      f"horizon-by-variable cells; ratio range "
      f"[{ratio.min():.3f}, {ratio.max():.3f}]")
```

It is worth being explicit about what the figure does and does not license. The curves are
computed on the same out-of-sample errors that will later be used to compare models, so
reading the minimum off the picture and then reporting the error at that minimum as the
model's performance would be using the evaluation sample twice. The defensible reading is
the shape rather than the argmin: over three orders of magnitude of $\lambda_1$ every value
beats the unrestricted system, and the curve is flat enough near its bottom that the exact
choice is not worth agonising over. That flatness is itself the practical content of R-6.1,
which says the error is quadratic in the neighbourhood of the optimum and strictly
decreasing at zero shrinkage, so a wrong but reasonable $\lambda_1$ costs very little while
no shrinkage at all costs a great deal. The value $\lambda_1 = 0.03$ used below is chosen
as a round number in the middle of the useful range rather than as the winner of the sweep.

The three panels tell one story with three endings. The random walk is the worst model
for output growth and inflation at every horizon and gets steadily worse, which is what
a naive persistence forecast does to a series that is nearly mean-reverting at monthly
frequency; for the funds rate it is competitive at short horizons and falls behind only
later, because the policy rate genuinely is close to a random walk over a month or two.
The unrestricted system beats the random walk on the two growth rates but is beaten by
every other model almost everywhere, and the gap does not close as the sample grows,
because the window expands while the parameter count stays at $111$ and the extra
observations are spread across several regimes rather than concentrated in one.

The Minnesota system improves on the unrestricted one in all thirty-six
horizon-by-variable cells, by between two and sixteen percent. Against the AR(1) the
verdict is more honest than flattering. At twelve months the funds rate error of
$1.4605$ is the lowest of the four models, below the AR(1)'s $1.5154$, the unrestricted
system's $1.5466$ and the random walk's $1.5540$; but for output growth the univariate
benchmark is marginally better at every horizon, $1.2397$ against $1.2453$ at one month,
and marginally better for inflation too, $0.2717$ against $0.2774$ at one month. The
cross-variable information in this three-variable system is therefore worth very little
for forecasting those two series at monthly frequency, and a great deal for the policy
rate at long horizons, which is where one would expect it, because the policy rate
responds to output and prices and a univariate model cannot see that. Shrinkage does not
manufacture forecasting power out of nothing. It makes a richly parameterised system
usable at all, and the system is then only as informative as the economics inside it.

Two details of the table repay attention because they recur throughout the course. The
first is that the ranking of models depends on the horizon: the random walk is competitive
for the funds rate at one month and hopeless at twelve, while the unrestricted system is
mediocre everywhere and worst where the data are thinnest. A comparison run at a single
horizon would have supported a different conclusion, and the same caution applies to
comparisons run on a single variable. The second is that the Minnesota system is never the
worst model in any cell and never dramatically the best. That is the characteristic
signature of a shrinkage estimator, which buys insurance against the bad cases at a small
premium paid in the good ones, and it is exactly what the mean squared error decomposition
of R-6.1 predicts once $\lambda$ is set somewhere in the interior.

## Discussion: better forecasts, and not one shock with a name {#sec-discussion}

The central bank's question was how much history a forecast should use, and the answer
turns out to be that the question was the wrong one. All of it can be used, provided the
belief attached to it is graded: $111$ coefficients on $120$ observations is not too many
coefficients but too few restrictions, and R-6.3 supplies the restrictions with two
numbers rather than with a shorter lag length. The unrestricted system was beaten by a
random walk one step ahead; the shrunk system beats the unrestricted one in every cell of
a thirty-six cell table and beats the random walk everywhere except the very short
horizon for the funds rate.

The check against something already known is the behaviour of the shrinkage matrix
itself. R-6.2 says that $W$ tends to the identity as the sample precision rises, so the
eigenvalues of $W$, each one the fraction of the least-squares content retained along one
direction, must move towards one as the estimation window grows. That is a claim about a
$111 \times 111$ matrix which can be evaluated directly, once at the first forecast origin
with $108$ observations and once at the last with $424$.

```{python}
#| label: fig-shrinkage-spectrum
#| fig-cap: "The 111 eigenvalues of the shrinkage matrix W, sorted, at the first forecast origin and at the last. Each value is the fraction of the least-squares estimate retained along one direction of the design."
def shrink_spectrum(upto, lam1):
    D = mac.loc["1990-01":upto].to_numpy()
    Xo, Yo = build_var_xy(D, p_var)
    B_o = np.linalg.solve(Xo.T @ Xo, Xo.T @ Yo)
    r_o = Yo - Xo @ B_o
    Sig_o = r_o.T @ r_o / (Xo.shape[0] - Xo.shape[1])
    _, V0 = minn_prior_pieces(m_var, p_var, D.std(axis=0, ddof=1), lam1, 0.5,
                              100.0, np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]))
    samp = np.kron(np.linalg.inv(Sig_o), Xo.T @ Xo)
    W = np.linalg.solve(np.diag(1.0 / V0.ravel(order="F")) + samp, samp)
    return np.sort(np.linalg.eigvals(W).real)[::-1], Xo.shape[0]

w_early, n_early = shrink_spectrum(origins[0], lam_show)
w_late, n_late = shrink_spectrum(origins[-1], lam_show)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(np.arange(1, w_early.size + 1), w_early, "-o", ms=3,
        label=f"first origin, {n_early} observations")
ax.plot(np.arange(1, w_late.size + 1), w_late, "-s", ms=3,
        label=f"last origin, {n_late} observations")
ax.axhline(1.0, color="black", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("eigenvalue rank"); ax.set_ylabel("weight kept on least squares")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("The shrinkage matrix relaxes as the sample grows")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"mean eigenvalue of W: first origin {w_early.mean():.4f}, "
      f"last origin {w_late.mean():.4f}")
print(f"eigenvalues above 0.9: first origin {(w_early > 0.9).sum()}, "
      f"last origin {(w_late > 0.9).sum()}")
print(f"eigenvalues below 0.1: first origin {(w_early < 0.1).sum()}, "
      f"last origin {(w_late < 0.1).sum()}")

half = len(err[("ols", 1)]) // 2
early = rmsfe(f"minn{lam_show:g}", slice(0, half)) / rmsfe("ols", slice(0, half))
late = rmsfe(f"minn{lam_show:g}", slice(half, None)) / rmsfe("ols", slice(half, None))
print(f"mean forecast-error ratio over horizons, early origins "
      f"{np.round(early.mean(axis=0), 4)}, late origins {np.round(late.mean(axis=0), 4)}")
```

The two curves are R-6.2 in a picture. At the first origin the mean eigenvalue of $W$ is
$0.3031$ and only $12$ of the $111$ directions keep more than nine tenths of their
least-squares content, while $56$ keep less than one tenth: the prior is doing most of
the work. Four hundred and twenty-four observations later the mean has risen to $0.4293$,
$31$ directions are above nine tenths and $39$ below one tenth. The matrix is relaxing
towards the identity exactly as the result requires, and it is the same arithmetic as the
scalar weight $w = n_0/(n_0+n)$ of Lecture 1, with a matrix in place of a number.

The forecast errors tell a less tidy story, and the discrepancy is worth keeping. The
Minnesota advantage over least squares does narrow for output growth between the first
and second halves of the origins, its mean ratio rising from $0.9251$ to $0.9389$, but it
widens for inflation, from $0.9138$ to $0.8658$, and widens slightly for the funds rate
too, from $0.9583$ to $0.9410$. The reason is that the second half contains 2020, whose
observations are so far outside anything the 1990s and 2000s contain that an unrestricted
fit deteriorates faster than the extra sample size repairs it. Shrinkage is a loan against
information the sample does not yet have, repaid as the sample arrives, but only if the
arriving observations resemble the earlier ones. Lecture 12 is where that assumption is
dropped.

There is also a limitation that no amount of data repairs, and it is the reason for the
next chapter. Everything above is a statement about forecasting: which model predicts
the next twelve months with the smallest error. Not one sentence of it is a statement
about cause. The estimated system says that a high funds rate this month is followed by
lower output in eight months, but it cannot say whether that is the effect of policy on
the economy or the effect of the economy on policy, because both are present in every
coefficient and the residuals of the three equations are correlated with each other. A
central bank that wants to know what its own surprise decision does cannot read the
answer off a reduced-form fit, however well shrunk. The shrunk model forecasts well and
says nothing about which shock caused what. Lecture 7 takes this same posterior and this
same panel and adds the piece that is missing, the map from the reduced-form residual
covariance to a set of structural shocks, and shows that the map is not determined by
the data at all.

## Exercises

These are the chapter's practice questions; the [Week 6 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/06-minnesota-priors.qmd) works through them and adds the
lab.

1. By hand. Starting from R-6.2, show that the posterior precision is the sum of the
   prior precision and the sample precision, and that adding a second batch of data
   using the first posterior as prior gives the same answer as pooling both batches
   against the original prior. Then take $B_0 = \tau^2 I_k$ and $X^\top X = nI_k$ and
   show that every coefficient is shrunk by the common factor $n/(n + \sigma^2/\tau^2)$,
   identifying the value of $\tau$ at which exactly half the least-squares estimate
   survives.

2. Computational. Reproduce the tightness sweep of @sec-empirical with $\lambda_2$ set
   to $0.1$, $0.5$ and $1.0$ in turn, holding everything else fixed, and report for each
   the best $\lambda_1$ and the one-month-ahead error of the three variables. Then repeat
   the exercise with the scale ratios $\sigma_i/\sigma_j$ removed from R-6.3 and explain,
   using the units step of the derivation, why the funds rate equation deteriorates far
   more than the other two.

3. On real data. Add the ten-year Treasury yield from the same file as a fourth variable,
   which raises the system to $196$ coefficients, and rerun the comparison of
   @sec-empirical. Report whether the Minnesota system still beats the unrestricted one
   in every cell, whether the best $\lambda_1$ moves, and say in one paragraph whether
   the fourth variable improves the forecasts of the original three.

Exercise 1 is the one to attempt before the session, since the sequential-updating
property is used without comment in Lecture 7. Exercises 2 and 3 are written for the
session itself and reuse the code of @sec-empirical with the prior function changed.

## Reading and references

The regularisation material and the ridge equivalence in R-6.2 follow UPM Class 5. The
Minnesota specification of R-6.3, its two tuning numbers and the standard-deviation
parameterisation follow SGPE Lecture 4, pages 13 to 23, and Bańbura, Giannone and
Reichlin (2010), which is the scheduled reading and the source of the convention that
differenced variables take a prior mean of zero on their own first lag. Bauwens (2013),
Chapter 4, connects the single-equation regression priors of Lecture 2 with their system
counterparts and is the bridge to Lecture 7. The mean squared error decomposition behind
R-6.1 is standard; Chapter 3 of Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman gives the same argument
in the language of the singular value decomposition.

The evidence that dense shrinkage of this kind outperforms sparse variable selection on
economic data, the illusion of sparsity, is Giannone, Lenza and Primiceri (2021) and is
taken up in the Week 6 exercise session; Lecture 11 states the sparse alternative
properly. The data are the monthly FRED series distributed with this course as a
repository snapshot.

The explanations and exercises are adapted to this course's notation and weekly
structure; consult the cited originals for the full treatments.

Koop, *Bayesian Econometrics*, ch. 2-4. Chan, Koop, Poirier and Tobias, *Bayesian
Econometric Methods* (2nd ed.), ch. 2-4. Bańbura, Giannone and Reichlin (2010), "Large
Bayesian Vector Auto Regressions," *Journal of Applied Econometrics*. Giannone, Lenza and
Primiceri (2021), "Economic Predictions with Big Data: The Illusion of Sparsity,"
*Econometrica*.
